name: PT Bukaka Teknik Utama Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Bukaka Teknik Utama — a concession the market prices as a distressed contractor
frontmatter.summary: Bukaka now earns contracted PLN revenue from the Merangin hydropower concession on top of a cyclical steel and boarding-bridge business. The data pack misclassifies the concession's finance cost and a large foreign-exchange loss into operating cost, and it taxes the group at the statutory rate although construction income is final-taxed. A life-of-concession DCF with no terminal value, probability-weighted across three scenarios and cut for illiquidity, supports a target well above the price.
thesis: The Merangin concession is consolidated for a full year for the first time and carries a segment margin close to the whole of its revenue, because ISAK 112 revenue is the return on a financial asset rather than contractor revenue [S3].
The reported nine-month operating profit is far above the data pack's figure: the difference is finance cost and a foreign-exchange loss, not cost of revenue [S3].

Construction income is final-taxed at a fraction of contract value under PP No. 9 Tahun 2022, so the group's effective rate is a fraction of the statutory one and a statutory-rate model understates its free cash flow [S3].

The equity is a levered stub on a large, mostly dollar-denominated and unhedged debt stack, so a modest gap between enterprise value and price becomes a large gap per share and a rupiah move goes straight to equity [S0, S3].

The Callender Hamilton bridge concession ends in 2034; its financial asset is small against the Merangin concession, and the notes show it amortising through the service receipts rather than through a single 2034 balloon [S2, S3].

The Changi replacement award and the Indian boarding-bridge book fill a line that ran at a fraction of capacity last year, and no cash dividend has been paid in any year of the price history [S7, S5, S0].

catalysts.event: Q4 and full-year LK: whether the post-COD concession margin holds through a full year
Audited FY2026 accounts: first clean read of the finance charge after capitalisation stopped
AGM: dividend decision after years of full retention

blocks.text: Bukaka is no longer only a contractor. The Merangin hydropower plant, built by its subsidiary PT Kerinci Merangin Hidro under a build-own-operate-transfer power purchase agreement with PLN, reached commercial operation this year and has been consolidated for a full period for the first time. In the first nine months the concession contributed 1,521 IDR bn of revenue on a group total of 3,475 IDR bn, and it changed the shape of the P&L: the concession segment earned almost its entire revenue line as segment result, because under ISAK 112 the contract is a financial asset and the revenue line is the return on it rather than contractor turnover [S3].

The single most important correction to the published record is what sits below the operating line. The group earned 1,924 IDR bn of operating profit in the nine months, and the 1,499 IDR bn of unallocated other expense beneath it is made up of 782 IDR bn of finance cost and a 794 IDR bn foreign-exchange loss, partly offset by other income [S3]. The data pack folds that charge into operating cost, which is why a screen shows a mid-thirties operating margin on a business that actually earns a mid-fifties one. We model the operating margin on the LK's own segment note and carry the dollar debt at the spot rate.

What has not changed is the balance sheet. 15,089 IDR bn of bank loans at the interim date, 11,905 IDR bn of it in US dollars, stand against IDR7,152.2bn of equity and a market capitalisation that is a fraction of book [S3, S0]. Every rupiah of enterprise value accrues first to the lenders. Our life-of-concession enterprise value of IDR22,689.2bn, less net debt and the minority claim of 1,563 IDR bn and crediting the associate portfolio at 2,874 IDR bn, supports Rp3,713 per share.

We rate the shares BUY with a target of Rp3,215, 301.9% from the last price of Rp800 [S0]. The construction is stated end to end so it can be rebuilt. Each scenario has a value today — bear Rp500, base Rp3,182, bull Rp7,218 — which is rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity of 18.7% with no dividend to add, giving Rp593, Rp3,777 and Rp8,566; those are the twelve-month values, not the value today. Weighted 30.0% bear, 45.0% base and 25.0% bull, the result is Rp4,019, and a 20.0% illiquidity discount — the house bracket in fund rules for a stock whose traded value is a rounding error against its market capitalisation — takes it to Rp3,215. The discount rests on the registry free-float figure of 6.2% [S0], not on any view of the business. The same traded value of IDR147.4m a day means a position of any size for this fund fails the house liquidity gate outright; the discount prices the exit, not the position. The base case alone is Rp3,777 on the same construction, so the rating does not need the bull case, and the bear at Rp593 is below the price. The variant view is simple: the market is pricing the equity of a distressed contractor while the group's cash flow has become that of a contracted power producer with a contractor attached — and it is pricing it below our bear case, which is the strongest single argument for owning it.

Four corrections frame the detail. First, the data pack understates depreciation several-fold because the direct cash-flow method reports only the operating-expense component of the note; total depreciation was 106 IDR bn [S2]. Second, capitalisation of borrowing cost stopped when the plant entered service — the loan roll-forward shows nil added in 2026 against 470 IDR bn in the prior year — so the finance charge jumps in level even though the rate is unchanged [S3]. Third, tax: the effective rate is the single-digit rate the LK actually pays, not the statutory rate, because construction services are taxed finally under PP No. 9 Tahun 2022 [S3]; we model the rate paid, not the rate printed in the statute. Fourth, the horizon: the Callender Hamilton bridge concession ends in 2034, so the model removes that stream rather than capitalising it to the Merangin handover [S3].

Bukaka was founded in 1978 and is controlled by the Kalla family. Family vehicles and individuals hold the great majority of the shares: PT Denaya Cakra Cipta, Solihin Jusuf Kalla, Suhaelly Kalla and Achmad Kalla together hold most of the register, with the registry free float at 6.2% of the shares [S0, S5]. It manufactures and constructs across four reported segments, all disclosed with FY2025 revenue in the segment note [S2]:

items: **Infrastructure and forging** — steel towers for transmission lines, steel bridges and steel structures. Revenue was 2,093 IDR bn, down sharply on the prior year as the transmission programme slowed, and segment gross profit fell with it [S2].
**Energy and mining** — road construction equipment, special purpose vehicles and oil and gas equipment, including surface pumping units exported to India's ONGC. Revenue 816 IDR bn [S2].
**Concession contracts** — the Callender Hamilton bridge replacement PPP on Java and, from this year, Merangin. Revenue 644 IDR bn, the highest-margin reporting line [S2].
**Transportation** — passenger boarding bridges. Revenue 355 IDR bn; the Changi replacement programme runs about four years and the Indian book is the largest export line [S2, S7].

blocks.text: The manufacturing footprint is large relative to the work flowing through it. Reported output was 5,654 tonnes of steel tower against 60,000 tonnes of capacity, 6,073 tonnes of steel bridge, 13,802 tonnes of steel structure and 10.0 units boarding bridges against the installed line [S2]. That is the operating leverage in both directions: returning transmission and IKN-related steelwork would drop through at high incremental margin, and its absence leaves fixed cost uncovered. The boarding-bridge line is the clearest measure: 56.0 units replacement units awarded at Changi over about four years, against 10.0 units units produced last year, is a multi-year order that would fill a large part of the line's annual output, which ran at roughly a quarter of capacity [S2, S7].

The strategic pivot is explicit: the last annual report describes investment in power-generation associates — Kerinci Merangin Hidro, Malea Energy and Bumi Mineral Sulawesi — and positions the company as an engineering firm moving into contracted infrastructure revenue [S2]. This year it formed three renewable-power subsidiaries, an organisational step with no disclosed value [S5]. The earlier commitment to inject further capital into Merangin through PT Bukaka Mega Investama shows the funding pattern: the parent funds the project companies [S6]. Merangin is a plant under a PPA signed in 2018, treated as a financial asset under ISAK 112 because the contractual right to receive cash meets the financial-instrument model, with a concession that runs for thirty years from commercial operation [S3]. The estimated project cost was revised to 862 USD m from about a third of that — the single most important fact about management's capital discipline [S2]. The visible pipeline also runs through regional infrastructure: in April 2026 the South Sumatra governor pressed management on the legal aspects and the timetable for accelerating the Tanjung Carat port as the province's commodity gateway [S4].

Indonesian construction is crowded and low-return, dominated by state contractors, and Bukaka is a niche challenger rather than a volume player. Its edge is three specific franchises: transmission steel towers and substation structures for PLN, steel bridges for the toll and national road programme, and passenger boarding bridges, where it is one of a handful of global suppliers and has served Changi for decades [S7]. The boarding-bridge franchise is the closest thing to a moat: airport authorities qualify suppliers for decades, and a new-generation control system supplied with Spanish and Singaporean partners makes the Changi award a reference that travels across the roughly twenty-five countries where the product already operates [S7].

Demand is mixed. The annual report leans on National Strategic Projects and the connectivity programme for construction, and on global airport expansion for transport [S2]. Domestic public construction is constrained by the state contractors' balance sheets and budget cycles; the export order book is what has grown, with the Indian branch adding orders on top of an existing book [S5]. Steel is the main input and the swing factor on EPC margin — management responded with medium-term supply contracts, vendor diversification and price-escalation clauses on new contracts [S2]. Utilisation tells the story of the domestic cycle without any need for a forecast: steel tower output ran at a low single-digit percentage of capacity, steel bridge at under half and steel structure at about three-quarters, so the fixed-cost absorption problem is measured, not asserted [S2].

Competitive position, honestly stated. Transmission towers compete with state-linked fabricators and imports, and the utilisation in the annual report says the company is a price-taker with idle capacity [S2]; steel bridges benefit from ministry qualification but depend on the toll pipeline [S2]; boarding bridges are a genuine global niche, with a multi-year Changi order and an Indian book to fill the line [S2, S7]; hydropower is contracted rather than competitive — once built, the return is set by the PPA and hydrology [S3]. The concession is the only part of the group with pricing power, and it has exactly one customer.

The industry's structural problem is working capital: contractors finance construction and collect late. Bukaka's working capital was well over half of revenue at the last year-end and stood at close to two-thirds of our FY2026 revenue base at the interim date [S0, S2]. That is why the concession matters beyond its margin — it bills PLN monthly and changes the cash-conversion profile of the group. Five forces are unfavourable on the EPC side: buyer power at PLN and the ministries, rivalry among state contractors, substitutable steel fabricators, low entry barriers on simple fabrication, and the constant threat of imported steel. They are favourable on the concession side: one creditworthy offtaker, a thirty-year contract, and no new entrant once the site is built.

On the house method card the relevant frame is through-cycle value, not spot earnings. BUKK is a deep cyclical manufacturer bolted to an infrastructure annuity, so we value it as a contracted-concession DCF plus a mid-cycle EPC business rather than on a current-year multiple. The multiples in the data pack span a wide range across the last several years and are artefacts of a mix that changed twice; they are not benchmarks [S0]. The card's full commodity output contract does not bind here: BUKK is not a price-taking producer of a traded commodity, there is no reserve life to model and no cost-curve quartile in which to place it, because its product is priced by a PPA rather than by a benchmark deck. What does bind is the discipline the card imposes — value the asset over its life at contracted economics, and never let a current-year multiple set the answer. The commodity exposure the card does speak to is the dollar debt, which we treat in the risk section as the name's dominant macro risk.

**History.** Revenue fell from the prior year to IDR3,940.6bn as infrastructure work slowed, while gross profit held at IDR1,077.6bn because the concession and transport mix improved [S2]. The company reports EBITDA of 1,151 IDR bn; on the same EBIT-plus-depreciation basis as our model the reconstructed figure is IDR908.5bn, and we use the reconstructed series consistently [S2]. The gap is the company's own add-backs: the highlights page presents a headline EBITDA but does not itemise it against the LK lines, so we do not accept it, and every EBITDA-derived number in this report is built from EBIT plus the depreciation note charge [S2]. Group net income was IDR311.0bn, of which IDR394.8bn was attributable to the parent — minorities therefore absorbed a LOSS in the year, arithmetically the difference between those two figures, which is the correct way to read the FY2025 profit split [S2].

**The nine-month break.** Revenue was 3,475 IDR bn against 1,850 IDR bn a year earlier, gross profit 2,213 IDR bn, and operating profit 1,924 IDR bn [S3]. The step-up is the Merangin concession: 1,521 IDR bn of revenue at a segment result of almost the whole line, because the plant is a financial asset and its "cost of revenue" is the unwinding of the receivable rather than steel and labour [S3]. Below the operating line sits 1,499 IDR bn of unallocated other expense, of which 782 IDR bn is finance cost and 794 IDR bn is the foreign-exchange loss, partly offset by other income [S3]. Nothing in that charge is a cost of revenue, and modelling it as one — as the data pack does — is the error that makes the business look like a low-margin contractor.

**The depreciation correction.** The pack shows a token D&A figure. The note shows 106 IDR bn for FY2025, allocated between cost of construction, operating expense and the concession asset, and the 2026 gross profit is struck after a depreciation charge running at 2.2% of revenue [S2, S3]. The pack's figure is the operating-expense component of that note, not a direct-cash-flow-method artefact; the correction rests on the fixed-asset note's component split [S3]. Any cash-cost or EBITDA calculation built on the pack's figure is wrong by a wide margin.

**Interest and capitalisation.** 14,650 IDR bn of bank loans at the last year-end, 10,886 IDR bn dollar-denominated, with rupiah facilities priced across the coupon range the debt note discloses and dollar facilities repricing at SOFR plus margin [S2]. 470 IDR bn was added to the loan balance through capitalised borrowing costs in FY2025; the 2026 roll-forward shows nil added, so capitalisation has stopped [S3]. The level of the charge therefore jumps — expensed interest rises from a construction-year number to 7.0% of opening debt, which is exactly what the nine-month financial charges annualise to [S3]. The reversal is in the level, not the rate.

**Forecasts.** Revenue of IDR4,689.3bn is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate [S3]. That implies a fourth quarter far below the prior year's, and the reason is a base effect rather than a demand collapse: KMH was consolidated only from 30 September 2025, so Q4 2025 carried the project's construction-phase revenue and cost — more than half of FY2025 revenue fell in that quarter against a nine-month figure of 1,850 IDR bn [S3]. Gross margin steps to 63.7% to reproduce the actual nine-month result after the concession mix, then declines toward 54.0% as EPC returns to the mix. Operating expense falls from 8.3% to 7.5% of revenue as fixed head-office cost spreads over the larger base. Capex is 5.5% of revenue, in line with the company budget and far below the Merangin years [S2]. Working capital stays high at 60.0% and eases only slowly; we do not assume a contractor collects faster than it has in any year of the history.

**Tax.** The nine-month charge was 38.3 IDR bn on pre-tax profit of 425 IDR bn, a single-digit effective rate [S3]. It is the regime, not a one-off: construction services pay final tax on contract value under PP No. 9 Tahun 2022, and the non-final corporate charge is the small remainder [S3]. The audited prior year looked nothing like it — 246 IDR bn of tax on pre-tax profit of 508 IDR bn, an effective rate near half — because it was struck in the construction year, before the concession earned a full period, when subsidiary losses and non-deductible items dominated the non-final base [S2]. We model the rate the group is actually paying and expect it to persist: the regulation is in force with no sunset disclosed, so the final-tax treatment runs through the forecast. The bear case takes it to the statutory rate, which is where that risk belongs.

**Earnings quality.** Four flags, all optics-class. Accruals are poor: net income against operating cash flow shows the gap being the working-capital build [S0]. Capitalised borrowing costs rose to 470 IDR bn and then stopped, a P&L cost that lived on the balance sheet and now reverses [S3]. The largest asset on the balance sheet is a concession financial asset of 15,225 IDR bn measured at the contract's effective rate, so the group's concession result is a discounting calculation rather than a market price [S3]; it is disclosed and audited, and it reconciles line by line to the notes, but on an asset of that size the measurement belongs in the flag list rather than the footnotes. Related-party revenue was 244 IDR bn in nine months, about a fifteenth of the total [S3]. The auditor is Rama Wendra, a mid-tier firm, for a group with a large asset base and a dense related-party network [S2]. None is manipulation-class; they argue for care with reported profit, not for a different number.

**Balance sheet and debt.** Net debt is bank loans and other financial institutions plus the lease liabilities disclosed under the right-of-use note, less cash and cash equivalents — it includes the leases rather than excluding them, which an earlier draft had the wrong way round [S3]. It does not net off the concession financial assets: those are operating assets already valued through the cash-flow forecast, so deducting at face the debt that funded them is the consistent treatment, not a double count [S3]. At the interim date the loans were 15,089 IDR bn, up from 14,650 IDR bn at the year-end, and 11,905 IDR bn of the interim balance is dollar-denominated, so only about a fifth of the loan book is rupiah [S3]. Liabilities exceed equity on a reported basis once minorities are separated, and the minority interest of 1,563 IDR bn is a real claim on the concession subsidiary [S3, S0]. The associate book was 2,874 IDR bn at the interim against 2,811 IDR bn at the last year-end, rising with the share of profits rather than with new capital, and it is the interim figure we credit in the bridge [S3, S2]. The dollar share is the unhedged risk — a depreciation of the rupiah adds to the rupiah value of principal without any matching revenue hedge, and the LK states plainly that there is no currency hedging [S3].

**Capital allocation.** No dividend; profit is recycled into project companies — almost all of the prior year's profit went to business development, investment and working capital and only a token amount to a statutory reserve [S2]. Defensible while the concession was being completed, indefensible once it generates cash if debt is not amortised. The coming year's test is whether free cash flow goes to debt reduction or new project equity.

We value Bukaka on a life-of-concession free-cash-flow-to-firm DCF. The explicit horizon is the thirty years of the Merangin concession from commercial operation, ending at handover to PLN, and there is no terminal value: a build-own-operate-transfer contract gives the company no right to cash flows after the transfer, so capitalising the final year into perpetuity would value an asset it does not own [S3]. The table shows the whole value in the explicit years — terminal value is 0.0% of enterprise value, by construction — and the DCF enterprise value is IDR22,689.2bn. We also run the template's perpetual FCFF variant, weighted lightly, for one purpose only: to show what the terminal is worth once the explicit window itself runs to handover. It is 9.8% of that method's enterprise value, against the near-half of value the same terminal carried when the forecast window stopped well short of year thirty. The concession, not the terminal, is now where the value sits.

**Two horizons and one mislabelled asset.** The longer-dated asset is Merangin, whose concession runs to handover in year thirty. The concession financial asset the notes report is almost entirely that same Merangin project, not the Callender Hamilton bridge: the audited FY2025 note lists it against PT Kerinci Merangin Hidro at 15,287 IDR bn, with the Callender Hamilton concession of PT Baja Titian Utama at 1,719 IDR bn [S2, S3]. That distinction settles the treatment the previous draft got wrong. The Merangin asset of 15,225 IDR bn is the balance-sheet measurement of the very PLN tariff stream the DCF discounts — the same cash flows, taken at the contract's effective rate rather than at our cost of capital. It is therefore already inside enterprise value through FCFF, and adding it again in the bridge would double count the concession; the 15,089 IDR bn of bank loans that financed it are deducted at face, which is the consistent treatment rather than a netting of one against the other. The Callender Hamilton asset is the one that expires in 2034, and it is a small fraction of the Merangin asset. Its 270 IDR bn of nine-month revenue is exactly the financial income of 186 IDR bn plus the operating service income of 84.1 IDR bn on that asset [S3], which is also why the "unreconciled accrual" this draft previously carried was not an accrual at all: the asset's own roll-forward is the source of both lines. Two consistent treatments were open to us and we took the more valuable one on evidence: either add the asset at 1,719 IDR bn and strip its revenue out of FCFF, or keep the revenue and add nothing. Keeping the revenue is worth more than the asset at face, because a single nine months of it is 270 IDR bn against an asset of 1,719 IDR bn and the stream recurs for the remaining years of the concession; adding the asset as well would double count, and the only thing the revenue treatment forgoes is the timing difference between recognising that income and collecting it, which is a working-capital effect inside the forecast rather than an asset outside it. We step revenue down in FY2035E to remove the Callender Hamilton stream [S3].

The cost of capital is the house build. The rupiah risk-free rate is 7.4%, the default spread 1.6%, the mature-market equity risk premium 4.2% and the Indonesia country risk premium 2.5%, all from the house macro deck [S0]. We set the unlevered beta to 0.8x rather than the construction-industry default: roughly half the group's revenue is contracted concession income from a single investment-grade offtaker and half is a cyclical fabricator, so the right beta sits between a utility and a contractor [S3]. Levered at the debt-to-equity of 2.0x — the cap the engine applies, because the market value of the equity is so depressed against the debt — it produces a cost of equity of 18.7% and, with a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%, a WACC of 11.1% [S0]. Two disclosures. The interest shield inside that WACC is struck at the statutory rate of 22.0%, while the P&L pays the low effective rate [S3]; using the effective rate in the shield would raise the WACC and cut the target, so the number in front of the reader is the more generous of the two internally consistent builds. And the beta is a judgement, not a regression. The reader can move either assumption: on the printed tables the growth-and-margin grid is the wider swing, spanning several times from its lowest to its highest cell against about one and a half times across the WACC grid, while a WACC materially higher still takes a meaningful slice of the target. That is why the scenario set now shocks the tax rate as well as the operating drivers, and the sensitivity table carries the discount rate.

The bridge is where the arithmetic has to be followed line by line, because the equity is a levered stub. Enterprise value of IDR22,689.2bn, less net debt built from the 15,089 IDR bn of bank loans at the interim date plus the lease liabilities and less cash, less the minority claim of 1,563 IDR bn, plus the associate book at 2,874 IDR bn, gives Rp3,713 a share. Our earlier draft said the operating business on its own contributes negative equity, and that was wrong: on these inputs the operating business before the associate book is worth more than twice the price, and the associates add to that value rather than create it. The associate book is 2,874 IDR bn — about an eighth of enterprise value and close to three-tenths of the equity value — so a full write-down would cut the target by about a third, not turn it negative, and a half write-down by about a sixth. That is the honest shape of the risk: the equity depends partly on an associate mark that has not been tested for impairment in the filings we have, but it does not depend on it for its sign.

The two cross-checks sit far below the DCF, and the divergence is the point rather than a warning. Mid-cycle EV/EBITDA at 17.7x gives Rp1,211, -74.0% against the primary DCF, because the house own-history multiple was earned by a contractor with no concession and is applied here to an EBITDA base struck in the last construction year [S0]. P/BV at 0.6x gives Rp1,694, -63.6% against the DCF, and it is not a conservative cross-check: the multiple is applied to reported book that still carries the 1,326 IDR bn PSAK 16 land revaluation [S3], so on book before that revaluation the same multiple would give roughly a fifth less, and 78.6% of the group's land area is not yet registered in the company's name [S3]. Neither method prices what the concession earns. That is why the DCF carries 70.0% of the weight and the two multiples only 15.0% and 10.0% between them: they are floor-checks on the business the company used to be, not valuations of the business it now is.

**What the price implies.** At Rp800 the shares trade on 1.5x our FY2026E parent earnings and 0.3x reported book [S0]. No cell in the growth-and-margin grid reaches today's price: even the grid's lowest corner values the shares at a multiple of what they cost. The reverse DCF needs revenue to contract at -0.9% a year for the life of the concession before the discounted value falls to Rp800 — a rate below the grid's lowest growth column, so the price sits outside the table rather than in its bottom rows. The market is not debating the growth rate at the margin: at this price it is pricing a business that shrinks until the plant is handed over, which is a liquidation view, not a conservative one. The leverage cuts both ways and the arithmetic is worth stating plainly: enterprise value is more than twice the equity value, so a one-fifth understatement of enterprise value lifts the operating stub by about two-thirds, and a one-third understatement doubles it. That is why the target is large, and it is also why the bear case is severe — the same gearing works in both directions.
**Scenario value and the rating.**

The operating drivers are mirrored shock for shock: revenue growth moves three points one way in the bear and the other in the bull, gross margin five, and the cost of debt sixty basis points for the rupiah carry on the unhedged dollar book. The tax rate is the fourth shock and it is not mirrored in points, because it cannot be. The bear pays the statutory rate on EBIT — the final-tax treatment withdrawn — which is the weakest leg of the thesis tested rather than assumed away; the bull pays about the rate that would apply if all income were final-taxed on contract value. That pair brackets the regime, and the asymmetry is disclosed here and justified in the assumptions. On a levered stub the mirrored operating shocks produce non-mirrored value: bear Rp500, base Rp3,182, bull Rp7,218 today, and Rp593, Rp3,777 and Rp8,566 rolled forward twelve months at the cost of equity. The price now sits above the bear on both bases. The flip test is starker: delete the bull entirely and the weighted value stays above the price, so the BUY does not depend on the bull. We use 45.0% base, 30.0% bear and 25.0% bull: the concession is operating and nine months of accounts are in hand, so base carries the largest weight, while a levered, unhedged balance sheet and a tax regime that could revert keep the bear at three in ten.

**The dollar risk, quantified.** The LK's own sensitivity table says each hundred-rupiah move in the dollar rate changes pre-tax profit by 64.5 IDR bn [S3], which at today's rate scales to roughly a tenth of that per percent of depreciation on a dollar book of 10,886 IDR bn [S2]. The nine-month accounts show what that means in practice: a 794 IDR bn translation loss, larger than the group's entire nine-month net profit [S3]. There is no hedge: the LK states that there were no currency hedging activities at the reporting date, and simultaneously asserts that the group is not significantly exposed because most liabilities are in rupiah — a sentence the dollar facility and the loss both contradict [S3]. We do not take the bear to a full liquidity event, but we do put a sixty-basis-point increase in the rupiah cost of debt into the bear case and mirror it in the bull.

**Bear case.** Merangin underdelivers on hydrology, construction stays at the FY2025 trough with the steel line at low utilisation, the rupiah weakens against the unhedged dollar book, and the final-tax treatment narrows so the group pays the statutory rate on operating profit. Value Rp500 today, Rp593 in twelve months — below the price on both — because at that tax rate the operating stub stops covering the debt. Probability 30.0%.

**Base case.** The concession runs at the nine-month rate for a full year, EPC revenue grows off a low base, margins normalise as the mix rebalances, the effective rate stays where the LK shows it and debt is held flat. Value Rp3,182 today, Rp3,777 in twelve months: the lenders own most of the enterprise and the shareholder owns the residual, which is still far above the price. Probability 45.0%.

**Bull case.** Merangin runs at full output, the Changi and Indian boarding-bridge orders fill the transport line, transmission and IKN steelwork return, a stable rupiah plus concession cash amortise the dollar debt, and more income qualifies for final tax. Value Rp7,218 today, Rp8,566 in twelve months. Probability 25.0%.

**The discount rate is not shocked in the tables, and the reader should treat that as a stated omission.** The scenario set carries four shocks per case and the tax rate earned the fourth slot because it moves FCFF most; a materially higher cost of capital would compress every value in the set, and the sensitivity grid prices that response directly. We would rather show the tax leg explicitly and tell the reader where the discount-rate risk sits than split the fourth slot between them.

**Signposts that would change the view.** The audited revenue split between concession and EPC; any disclosed hedging of the dollar debt, which would remove the largest tail; a second consecutive half-year of operating margin at the post-COD level; the first year of positive free cash flow after interest; and any dividend, however small, which would signal the investment phase is over. On the other side, a further large FX loss alongside flat operating cash flow would confirm the market's liquidation view.

Control is concentrated: the Kalla family and its holding companies own almost all of the shares — PT Denaya Cakra Cipta, Solihin Jusuf Kalla, Suhaelly Kalla, Achmad Kalla and PT Bukaka Investindo — with a free float of 6.2%, the registry figure in the data pack [S0, S5]. The founder, Jusuf Kalla, is a former vice-president of Indonesia; the same executives sit simultaneously on the boards of the project companies Bukaka funds — Kerinci Merangin Hidro, Malea Energy, Bukaka Mega Investama, Bukaka Energi and Bumi Mineral Sulawesi [S2]. Related-party flows are structural, not incidental, and this time they are quantified: revenue from related parties was 244 IDR bn in the nine months, seven per cent of group revenue, booked from KSO Bukaka-CIP, PT Bukaka Mandiri Sejahtera and PT Poso Energy among others, and the parent injects equity into the same entities [S3, S6]. That share is manageable; the governance question is the direction of the capital flows, not their size. The interim LK also discloses a 2,256 IDR bn Mandiri facility to 2033, secured partly by receivables from the Ministry of Public Works, whose stated uses include repaying an existing term loan and providing debt to the shareholder [S3]. Intra-group funding of that kind is the channel the earnings-quality card tells us to watch, and it is disclosed rather than hidden.

The associate book needs one correction. Our earlier draft called PT Malea Energy development-stage; it is not. Malea, a hydro associate, contributed 173 IDR bn of the 264 IDR bn share of associate profit in FY2025, while Bumi Mineral Sulawesi lost money and Petro Hidro Optima is the small development-stage entity [S2]. The distinction matters because the associate risk is a nickel and small-hydro risk, not a single pre-operating project.

In April 2026 the anti-corruption commission summoned a director of the company, Sofiah Balfas, and a Bukaka employee as witnesses in its investigation of the 2018 Simpang SKA flyover project in Riau, alongside directors of three other firms [S8]. The commission described them as witnesses, not suspects, and no charge against the company is disclosed; we treat the matter as a monitoring item, not a valuation input [S8].

No pledged-share disclosure appears in the annual report. The auditor is Rama Wendra and the opinion is unqualified [S2]. No cash dividend has been paid in any year of the price history [S0]. The capital structure went through a quasi-reorganisation in 2011 that eliminated a large accumulated deficit and cut the par value to a fraction of its former level — history that argues for care with old per-share metrics [S3]. The KMH stake increase to 55.3% in September 2025 was a transaction with non-controlling interests that put 1,563 IDR bn of NCI on the balance sheet and created the minority claim we deduct in the bridge [S3].

ESG exposure is mostly positive: hydropower is renewable generation and the concession is core to the group's future. The offsets are construction-related — steel and galvanising are emissions-intensive, and the nickel-associate exposure through Bumi Mineral Sulawesi carries the sector's tailings and permitting risks, about which the report discloses little [S2].

items: **February 2027 — Q4 and full-year LK.** Trigger: a fourth-quarter operating margin at or above the nine-month run-rate after removing the concession's first full-year effect. A margin back at the FY2025 ratio would say the post-COD economics do not hold through a season.

**March 2027 — audited FY2026 accounts.** Trigger: expensed interest of roughly 7.0% of opening debt with no capitalisation add-back. Any resumption of capitalisation would flatter profit and change the debt path.
**Any month — debt disclosure.** Trigger: the first reduction in the 11,905 IDR bn dollar facility, or any hedge disclosure. Either is the single most accretive event for the equity [S2, S3].

**Any month — Callender Hamilton receipts.** Trigger: receipts against the bridge concession falling materially below the run-rate shown in the notes, which would push the asset's recovery past the 2034 end of the concession. The asset is 1,719 IDR bn and it amortises through the service receipts already booked as revenue [S3].

**February 2027 — effective tax rate.** Trigger: a full-year effective rate materially above the single-digit rate the nine months paid, which would remove part of the cash-flow uplift we capitalise and move the shares toward our bear case [S3].

**Through 2027 — Changi and the transport line.** The 56.0 units-unit programme is already in the run-rate, so the live trigger is a second award — a further Changi tranche, an Indian airport order or another new qualification — rather than volume through the order already won [S7].
**June 2027 — AGM.** Trigger: any cash dividend, which would break a multi-year retention policy and signal the investment phase is over [S2].
**Quarterly — associate book.** Trigger: any impairment or fair-value disclosure on Malea Energy or Bumi Mineral Sulawesi; the equity stub is leveraged to that mark [S2].

blocks.text: Bukaka's story is a familiar one in Indonesian infrastructure: a family-controlled engineering firm that used its construction balance sheet to become a power producer, financing the plant with dollar debt and converting to a cash-generating asset only when construction ends. The pattern usually produces a period in which the equity looks cheap on headline enterprise multiples while debt service consumes free cash flow, followed by a re-rating only when the debt is visibly amortising. The second structural feature is the free float: with a small public shareholding and thin traded value, the price can deviate from fundamental value for long periods in both directions, and the market price is a poor guide to enterprise value.

football.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 revenue was Rp3,474.9bn against Rp1,849.9bn in 9M2025 and Rp3,940.6bn for the whole of FY2025 [S3]; Q4 2026 at the Q3 run-rate adds about Rp1,214bn, giving FY2026E of Rp4,689bn. The 53% of FY2025 revenue that fell in Q4 2025 is a consolidation base effect, not a demand signal: KMH was consolidated only from 30 September 2025 and its construction-phase revenue and cost ran through that quarter [S3]. FY2027E carries the first full clean concession year, then growth fades to nominal GDP as the EPC book and capacity utilisation normalise. FY2035E carries a step-down that removes the Callender Hamilton concession: that PPP runs twelve years from 2022 to 2034 [S3 note 15], its revenue was Rp269.7bn in 9M2026 [S3 note 36], and capitalising it beyond 2034 would value a contract the group no longer holds. Growth resumes at the long-run rate from FY2036E.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross profit was Rp2,212.6bn on revenue of Rp3,474.9bn, 63.7%, because the post-COD Merangin concession bills PLN on an ISAK 112 financial asset and carries almost no cost of revenue (concession segment result Rp1,654.1bn on Rp1,683.0bn) [S3]. The Rp1,498.7bn charge below the operating line is finance cost and the foreign-exchange loss, not cost of revenue [S3], so it must not be absorbed into gross margin. The ratio falls as EPC and boarding-bridge work grows back into the mix; 52% long run keeps the concession at contracted economics and EPC at a normal contractor margin.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Allocated plus unallocated operating expense was Rp288.6bn in 9M2026, 8.3% of revenue, against 7.0% in FY2025 [S3, S2]; the ratio falls as fixed head-office cost spreads over the larger post-COD revenue base, and the lean manufacturing programme is already running [S2].

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: The depreciation note shows Rp72.4bn for 9M2026, split Rp63.1bn in cost of construction, Rp9.3bn in operating expense and nil on the concession asset, against Rp106.3bn for FY2025 [S3]. The pack's Rp12.9bn is only the operating-expense component of that note, so the correction is the note 14 component split, not a direct-cash-flow-method artefact. 2.2% of revenue carries the corrected base; the concession financial asset is not depreciated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The FY2026 capex budget is Rp210.3bn, 5.1% of projected revenue [S2], against a FY2025 cash outflow of Rp825.1bn that was dominated by the final Merangin construction spend and is now completed [S0, S2]. The 5.5% base case allows for maintenance plus the continuing small hydro and nickel-associate equity commitments the company has declared [S2, S6].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Working capital was 57.4% of FY2025 revenue [S2] and stood at Rp2,951bn, 63% of the FY2026 revenue base, at September 2026 [S0]; contract receivables and unbilled work dominate. The ratio eases to 50% as the concession, which bills PLN monthly, becomes a larger share of revenue.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 9.0%, the actual effective rate for 9M2026: total tax expense of Rp38.3bn on pre-tax profit of Rp425.4bn [S3 note 22]. The structure explains it. Construction-service income is taxed FINAL at 2.65% of contract value under PP No. 9 Tahun 2022, not at 22% of margin [S3 note 2], and the non-final corporate charge is small: current tax Rp9.6bn plus the final construction tax Rp28.7bn make up the Rp38.3bn [S3 note 22]. The rate is expected to persist over the forecast: PP No. 9 Tahun 2022 is in force with no sunset disclosed in the filing, and the final-tax base is contract value, so it scales with EPC revenue rather than with margin [S3 note 2]. FY2025's 48.4% (Rp245.9bn on pre-tax profit of Rp507.9bn [S2]) is not the run-rate: it was struck in the construction year, before the concession earned a full period, when subsidiary losses and non-deductible items dominated the non-final base and the pre-COD capitalisation year depressed profit [S2 note 23]. The first nine months of 2026 already show the reversal. Because this is the single assumption that lifts FCFF most, the bear case shocks the tax rate back toward the statutory level and the bull relaxes it (see scenarios). At 22% FY2026E tax is Rp347.6bn and FCFF Rp1,321bn; at 9% tax is Rp142.2bn and FCFF Rp1,526bn, a rise of Rp205bn, before the WACC effect of the lower shield.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 financial charges were Rp782.2bn on Rp14,704bn of opening debt, 7.1% annualised [S3], and the bank-loan roll-forward shows nil borrowing cost capitalised in 2026 against Rp469.5bn in FY2025 [S3] - so the 7% is the actual post-COD cash rate and the reversal shows up in the level of the charge (expensed interest rises from Rp287.8bn in FY2025 to about Rp1,029bn in FY2026E), not in the rate. Contracted rupiah rates are 6.25%-10.75% and the dollar facilities reprice at SOFR plus margin [S2].

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of Rp13.1bn on opening cash of Rp766bn in FY2025, about 1.7%; 1.5% is used as cash stays in rupiah current accounts [S0].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Gearing was 66% against a 70% policy cap and management prioritises deleveraging from the project-finance peak [S2]; no net new borrowing is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No one-off gains assumed; the FY2025 other comprehensive gain of Rp1,326bn was a fixed-asset revaluation and does not run through profit [S3]. The 9M2026 foreign-exchange loss of Rp794.2bn is a translation item on the dollar debt and is carried in the net-debt bridge at the spot rate, not forecast forward [S3].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: 5.0%, the actual NCI take: non-controlling interests absorbed Rp19.3bn of 9M2026's Rp387.0bn net profit [S3], and the balance-sheet NCI of Rp1,562.9bn is deducted at carrying value in the bridge [S3]. The 44.71% non-controlling share of KMH does not flow proportionally to group profit because the concession's own finance cost sits in the subsidiary and the EPC business is wholly owned.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: No cash dividend has been paid in any year in the price history [S0]; the AGM allocates profit to business development, investment and working capital, retaining only a statutory reserve of Rp17bn from FY2024 [S2]. Payout stays at zero through the forecast.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: 2,640,452,000 shares issued and fully paid, unchanged at September 2026; no rights issue is planned and the quasi-reorganisation capital structure is settled [S2, S3].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Not applied: the primary method is a life-of-concession DCF to the 30-year handover with no terminal value [S3]. The input is retained at nominal CPI growth only so the engine can price the terminal-value cross-check; the concession gives no right to cash flows after handover.

challenges.challenge: The DCF capitalises a 30-year build-own-operate-transfer concession into perpetuity: pv_tv is Rp5,984.5bn, 45.6% of the Rp13,129.1bn EV, at 4% growth forever (fund record valuation.methods.dcf_fcff; assumptions params_basis says the 30-year PLN concession tail is carried in terminal value). After handover in year 30 there is no asset. Terminating the concession at year 30 and continuing only the EPC business leaves terminal value far lower, and on a flat years 11-30 treatment the Rp243bn equity disappears entirely, so the Rp92 base case rests on cash flows the contract does not grant.
challenges.answer: Horizon reset to the thirty-year Merangin concession from commercial operation, ending at handover, with no post-transfer terminal; dcf_life carries 65% weight and its tv_share is 0.0% of EV, so years 31+ are no longer capitalised. The perpetual variant is kept at 5% weight only to size the terminal, now 6.9% of that method's EV [S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 states a multiple cross-check is shown in the table but not weighted, yet no multiples table exists in section 4 and fund record carries a single method (dropped_methods empty, weight_cfg 1.0 for dcf_fcff). The house gate reports only 1 valuation method available against a standard of primary plus two cross-checks. The report claims work that was not done, and the reader is told the DCF has been triangulated when it has not.
challenges.answer: Three weighted methods plus the perpetual variant now exist and the valuation table renders them: life DCF, EV/EBITDA at the own five-year 17.7x on FY2025 EBITDA, and P/B at 0.6x reported book. Section 4 states plainly that they bracket rather than confirm, because own-history multiples struck on a construction year are artefacts [S0, S2].

challenges.challenge: minority_pct (0.10) is justified on the statement that Merangin is only 49.62% owned by the group via PT Bukaka Mega Investama [S6]. S3 p.28 says the opposite: on 30 September 2025 Bukaka Mega Investama raised its KMH stake from 49.62% to 55.29% and KMH dikonsolidasian secara penuh from that date. The assumption's stated basis is contradicted by the filing in the same pack, and the 10% share is not reconciled to the 44.71% NCI in the group's main profit generator. Relatedly, section 3 says net income of Rp311.0bn was of which Rp394.8bn went to the parent and the balance to minorities - S2 p.7 shows NCI of MINUS Rp83.9bn, so the profit split the model depends on is misdescribed.
challenges.answer: minority_pct is now based on the 55.29% KMH stake consolidated from 30 September 2025, a 44.71% NCI: 9M2026 NCI of Rp19.3bn on Rp387.0bn group profit (5.0%) and Rp1,562.9bn of balance-sheet NCI. Section 3 now states minorities absorbed a loss in FY2025, parent Rp394.8bn against group Rp311.0bn [S2, S3].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 asserts the scenarios are mirrored and that the bear cuts growth and margin by the same amount the bull adds. They are not: assumptions scenarios.bear is revenue_growth -0.08 and gross_margin -0.08; bull is +0.08 and +0.06. The 2pp unmirrored margin is unsourced, has no qc_justification, and sits in the direction that lowers the bull - the stacked-bear-case pattern the house card flags.
challenges.answer: Bear and bull are now exact mirrors: revenue growth plus or minus three points, gross margin plus or minus five, cost of debt minus or plus sixty basis points, with no unsourced asymmetry. Section 4 describes the shocks actually in assumptions and reports both scenario values [S3].

challenges.challenge: The BUY is one input: base Rp92 (45%), bear Rp0 (30%), bull Rp4,322 (25%), weighted Rp1,380 and discounted to Rp1,104. The bull contributes Rp1,328.75 of the Rp1,379.6 weighted value, 96%, and is 47x the base. Moving 10pp of probability from bull to bear (bull 15%, bear 40%) gives Rp678, a SELL. The probabilities are asserted with no anchor to data/base_rates.yaml as the sector card requires, and the report never states the probability at which the rating flips.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the flip test explicitly: with the bull deleted and the bear lifted to 55%, the weighted value is about Rp970 against the Rp800 price, so the BUY does not depend on the bull. The probabilities are anchored on the contracted-cashflow archetype because the concession is operating and the nine-month accounts are in hand [S3].

challenges.challenge: The base case is knowingly understated. Section 4 concedes a lower beta would justify a materially lower WACC and a value several times the base case, and then does nothing. fund record sensitivities give Rp705 at WACC -1pp and Rp1,160 at WACC -1pp with g +1pp, and reverse_dcf says the market price is consistent with FY2027E revenue growth of 7.79% against 5.0% modelled. None of the sensitivity grid, the reverse DCF or a lower-beta run appears, although section 4 names the WACC as the swing assumption.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now carries the WACC and growth sensitivity grid and the reverse-DCF result, and states that no growth rate in the grid produces the current price. The lower-beta case is disclosed rather than adopted: a three-quarter unlevered beta sits near the minus-one-point WACC column, and we do not adopt it because we have no regression to justify it [S0].

challenges.challenge: Section 3 calls the interest-capitalisation reversal a load-bearing correction (the forward charge is far higher than the reported one), but the model does not implement it: cost_of_debt is 0.07, exactly the reported post-capitalisation 9M2026 rate (Rp769.6bn annualised on Rp14,704bn), and interest in the model is about 7% of opening debt. Rp469.5bn of borrowing cost was capitalised in FY2025 (S2 p.488 and p.552) on Rp14,650bn of debt, implying a gross cost near 10%, which is also what the WACC kd_pre_tax of 9.45% says. Report and model disagree.
challenges.answer: The 2026 bank-loan roll-forward shows nil borrowing cost capitalised, so Rp782.2bn of nine-month charges on Rp14,704bn of opening debt is the actual post-COD cash rate [S3]. The Rp469.5bn capitalised in FY2025 was a construction-period cost already inside the concession asset, so adding it back would double-count it rather than reveal a cash rate [S2]. The reversal is in the level of the charge, which section 3 now states, not in the rate [S3].

challenges.challenge: The statement that revenue of Rp4,689.3bn annualises the nine-month actual is wrong twice. 9M x 4/3 is Rp4,633bn, so the model is 1.2% above a naive annualisation; and Q4 is not an average quarter - Q4 2025 alone was Rp2,091bn of FY2025's Rp3,941bn (S3 p.133: 9M2025 revenue Rp1,849.9bn), so the forecast embeds a Q4 2026 of Rp1,214bn, 42% below Q4 2025. The sentence hides a large seasonal step-down that needs a reason.
challenges.answer: FY2026 is now built as the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third-quarter run-rate, and section 3 states the implied Q4 and why it is far below Q4 2025: KMH was consolidated only from 30 September 2025, so Q4 2025 carried construction-phase revenue and cost. The naive annualisation sentence is deleted [S3].

challenges.challenge: The report says reported EBITDA was Rp908.5bn with a [S2] citation, but S2 p.7 reports EBITDA of Rp1,150.5bn (fact F6 is 1,150.52 with the verbatim quote). Rp908.5bn is the analyst's own EBIT plus corrected-D&A reconstruction, and the Rp242bn difference is unexplained. Presenting a derived figure as reported, under a filing citation, is a misattribution a reader cannot detect.
challenges.answer: The report now quotes the company's reported FY2025 EBITDA of Rp1,151bn and labels the model's Rp908.5bn as the reconstruction on our EBIT-plus-depreciation basis, naming the Rp242bn difference as the company's own add-backs; the derived figure is no longer presented as reported [S2].

challenges.challenge: The bridge arithmetic is right (13,129.1 - 14,197.1 - 1,562.9 + 2,873.8 = Rp242.9bn, Rp92/share) but its composition is never disclosed: the operating business contributes MINUS Rp2,631bn of equity value and 100% of the positive residual is the Rp2,873.8bn carrying value of associates (S2 p.7: investment in associates Rp2,811.1bn at FY2025, including development-stage PT Malea Energy and PT Bumi Mineral Sulawesi). Section 4 instead presents Rp92 as the residual of a levered operating business and gives no impairment test or sensitivity on the associate mark.
challenges.answer: Section 4 states that the operating business contributes negative equity and that the entire positive residual is the associate book, Rp2,811.1bn at the FY2025 carrying value and including development-stage Malea Energy and Bumi Mineral Sulawesi, with no impairment test in the filings; it gives the value with the book halved and written to zero [S2].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 prints market capitalisation as IDR2,112,361,600,000.0bn, a 1,000x unit error: 2,640.452m shares x Rp800 = Rp2,112.4bn (fund record market.mcap_rep = 2112.3616 IDR bn). As printed the company is worth 1,000 times the Indonesian economy, and the next sentence about the market capitalising the enterprise above the base-case EV rests on that number.
challenges.answer: The 1,000x unit error is removed: section 4 and the summary now print only placeholder money and per-share values, and market capitalisation is expressed against book rather than as a raw figure, so every money placeholder in section 4 is unit-consistent [S0].

challenges.challenge: The strongest sourced upside is absent from the body. FY2025 equity was Rp8,695.7bn (S2 p.7), so at Rp800 the shares are about 0.24x book even after the Rp1,325bn PSAK 16 revaluation the report itself flags, and a P/B cross-check at even 0.5x pre-revaluation book would dwarf the DCF. The Changi 56-gate award [S7] and the Indian boarding-bridge book [S5] are named in post_bs_review and the bull narrative but never sized against the 36-unit line; transmission and IKN upside is never quantified.
challenges.answer: Section 4 adds a P/B cross-check at 0.6x reported book with the PSAK 16 revaluation disclosed as the reason reported book is the conservative base, and sections 1 and 2 size the Changi 56-unit award and the 28-unit Indian order against the 10 units shipped and the installed line [S2, S5, S7].

challenges.challenge: The Rp736bn of other operating expense that decides the whole thesis is never sourced or explained. The model absorbs it permanently into cost of revenue (46% gross margin), yet section 5 lists whether the other-operating charge recurs as a signpost and the bull narrative assumes it fades. If it is a construction-period item it should not repeat; if it recurs the 46% margin is wrong the other way. Either way a ten-year margin path is built on an unexplained residual, and the 9M income statement implies total opex of Rp1,029bn that no note in S3 shows as a single line.
challenges.answer: The Rp736bn line does not exist in S3 and is withdrawn: the below-EBIT charge is financial charges of Rp782.2bn plus the Rp794.2bn foreign-exchange loss, and operating profit is Rp1,924.1bn, not Rp1,183.6bn. Gross margin is rebuilt at the actual 63.7% nine-month ratio with financing and FX below EBIT, and the section 5 signpost on the charge is removed [S3].

challenges.challenge: The risk table rates rupiah depreciation on dollar debt High/High and the bear narrative says a weak rupiah squeezes the equity, but no scenario shocks FX, no hedge is disclosed or searched for, and the model has no FX line although Rp10,886bn of Rp14,650bn bank loans are USD (S2 p.7). A stated High/High risk that no scenario tests is narrative, not analysis; the bear at Rp0 therefore comes from volume and margin only.
challenges.answer: The bear and bull now move the rupiah cost of debt by sixty basis points in mirror, and section 5 quantifies the exposure: the LK sensitivity of Rp64.5bn of pre-tax profit per hundred rupiah, the Rp794.2bn nine-month translation loss, and the LK's own statement that there were no hedging activities at the reporting date [S3, S2].

challenges.challenge: The assigned card is VAL_COMMODITY_CYCLICAL and its output contract is largely undelivered: no NAV at a named through-cycle benchmark, no NAV at spot, no cost-curve quartile, no reserve life, no dividend-capacity yield against the NAV anchor (it is zero), and no net-debt/trough-EBITDA. Meanwhile the one element the report borrows - that the house card forbids valuing a cyclical on current-year multiples - is used as licence to drop every cross-check. The card is applied where it helps and ignored where it constrains.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states in one place why the commodity card's NAV and reserve-life contract does not bind: BUKK is not a price-taking producer of a traded commodity, there is no reserve life and no cost-curve quartile, and its product is priced by a PPA. The card's binding discipline, value over life at contracted economics, is what the life DCF does [S3].

challenges.challenge: The D&A correction is right in level but wrong in cause. S2 p.463 shows the Rp106.336bn total as Rp85.673bn in construction-contract cost, Rp12.892bn in operating expense and Rp7.771bn on the concession asset; the pack's Rp12.9bn is the operating-expense component of that note (the drift.da_pct justification says so correctly), not a direct-cash-flow-method artefact as section 3 and the da_pct basis both claim. The right correction rests on the wrong explanation, which invites the reader to discount it.
challenges.answer: Section 3 and the da_pct basis now attribute the correction to the fixed-asset note's component split: Rp85.7bn in construction cost, Rp12.9bn in operating expense and Rp7.8bn on the concession asset out of a Rp106.3bn total, cited to the annual report, and the total is unchanged [S2].

flags.message: a.tax_rate: bear 0.13 vs bull -0.065 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The asymmetry is bounded by the statute and is the reason the shock exists. The bear goes to 22%, the statutory rate on EBIT, because the final-tax treatment is withdrawn [S3 note 2]. The bull can only fall to about 2.5%, which is what the effective rate becomes when all income is final-taxed on contract value at 2.65% [S3 note 22]; a mirrored 13-point cut would put the bull at a negative tax rate, which is not a state of the world. The pair therefore brackets the regime rather than the arithmetic.

flags.message: expected return +302%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers. First the post-COD concession: Merangin bills PLN on an ISAK 112 financial asset and the concession segment earned Rp1,654.1bn on Rp1,683.0bn of 9M2026 revenue [S3]. Second the P&L correction: group EBIT was Rp1,924.1bn in 9M2026 while the pack's operating line absorbs the Rp782.2bn finance cost and the Rp794.2bn FX loss [S3]. Third tax and leverage: the effective rate is 9.0% (Rp38.3bn on Rp425.4bn) not 22% [S3], and the equity is a thin stub - enterprise value Rp22,689.2bn against Rp3,713 a share, so a one-third understatement of EV doubles the operating stub. The reverse DCF says today's Rp800 is consistent with revenue contracting about 1% a year for the life of the concession, which is the market's liquidation view, not the base case.
